newsitem.title: USA: U.S. NASD regulator adopts arbitration rules.
newsitem.headline: U.S. NASD regulator adopts arbitration rules.

text.p: The regulatory arm of National Association of Securities Dealers said it adopted new rules governing the way securities industry disputes are resolved through arbitration.
The NASD Regulation Inc board of directors approved several rules proposed last January by a panel led by former Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman David Ruder.

Under one rule, punitive damages will be subject to a cap of $750,000 or two times the compensatory damages, whichever is the smaller amount. The rules must still be approved by the NASD board and the SEC.
Other arbitration measures include doing away with the "eligibility" rule that calls for claims to be filed within six years of an event leading to a securities dispute.

The new provision, also subject to SEC approval, would allow cases to be brought up even it the alleged wrongdoing happened more than six years earlier. But there is no guarantee a particular case would finally go through the arbitration process.
Under the new plan, brokers or firms involved may object and the NASD regulators may hold a forum to determine whether the case should go to arbitration.

"The significance for investors is that we have improved the arbitration system in our attempts to maintain it as a swift and less costly means to resolve disputes," NASD Chairman Mary Alice Brophy told reporters in a conference call.
Punitive damages and eligibility issues involving arbitration disputes have long generated controversy in the securities industry and in the investment community.
The NASD has taken steps to revise arbitration policies in response to concerns that the current system has favored the industry over investors.
The NASD regulatory board also adopted a rule barring an issuer or promoter from paying a market maker to put out quotes in a stock.
It also created two registrant categories for government securities and corporate equity traders.
